strengths: Novel two-stage decomposition of fusion objective into interpretable grouping and approximation error components with solid theoretical backing (Theorems 1-2)
First systematic incorporation of neuron importance scores into model fusion with convincing ablation studies demonstrating consistent improvements
Strong experimental results in non-IID and sharded settings where baselines fail (Table 1: 84.5-84.6 vs OTFusion 43.4, vanilla 11.2), addressing an important practical problem in federated learning
Generalizes to arbitrary architectures without task-specific adaptation, unlike prior methods like OTFusion
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple data distribution scenarios with proper statistical rigor (multiple seeds, error bars)
Clear mathematical framework with detailed proofs and honest discussion of limitations in Section 6
weaknesses: Gradient-based variant exhibits concerning practical limitations: hyperparameter sensitive (requires different settings per scenario, Table 5), scales poorly with limited fusion data (38s→632s for 400→6000 samples), and underperforms linear variant on limited data
Unresolved design issue: uses plain MSE instead of weighted MSE because important neurons 'barely change' under weighting, contradicting core motivation for importance scores
Limited experimental scope: only CIFAR-10/100 with VGG11 and ViT; no ImageNet, larger models, or other modalities; knowledge distillation restricted to last layer only
Modest improvements in realistic full-dataset setting with marginal gains over ensemble baseline (Table 3: 72.7 zero-shot vs 75.3 ensemble) and identical performance after fine-tuning
Non-IID experimental design limitations: base models see only 10-20% of data leading to artificially weak baselines; 400 fusion samples from CIFAR-10 may not reflect realistic federated scenarios

Incomplete baseline comparisons: could not benchmark Transformer OTFusion (implementation difficulties), Git Re-Basin marked N/A for 4+ way splits, hyperparameter selection on test scenarios introduces bias
Substantial gap to ensemble remains even in best cases (e.g., 84.5 vs 87.5 in Table 1) raising questions about practical value given ensemble's known alternative of knowledge distillation
Theory-practice gap: strong theory only for linear levels; gradient variant for non-linear levels lacks theoretical justification beyond ad-hoc initialization strategy
20× runtime overhead compared to OTFusion (14.2s vs 0.7s, Table 6) and somewhat incremental contribution combining existing K-means/Hungarian matching with importance weighting

strengths: Addresses real gaps in prior work: reproducibility issues, inflated baselines, and limited non-IID evaluation; zero-shot fusion under distribution shift is practically important for federated learning
Solid theoretical framework with clean decomposition (Theorem 1) into interpretable grouping/approximation errors; Theorem 2 provides optimality (HF) and (9+ε)-approximation (KF) guarantees

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three training regimes (Sharded, Non-IID, Full-Dataset), multiple architectures (VGG, ViT, ResNet), and strong baselines; extensive ablations with proper statistical rigor (std deviations, multiple seeds)
Dramatic empirical improvements in challenging settings where baselines collapse (e.g., 54.4% vs 4.4% on CIFAR-100 ViT sharded 2-way), demonstrating practical value for FL scenarios
Strong reproducibility with open-source code commitment, detailed hyperparameters, complete implementation details, and transparent data partitioning procedures
Honest discussion of limitations: acknowledges hyperparameter sensitivity, data efficiency requirements, computational overhead, and theoretical gaps
weaknesses: Limited novelty: core components (neuron matching, K-means, importance weighting) are established; main contribution is reformulation and retrofitting, which is incremental rather than fundamental

Significant computational overhead (23× slower than OTFusion in some settings) not fully justified; cost-benefit analysis incomplete, especially for full-dataset settings where improvements are modest

Large theory-practice gap: Theorem 2's (9+ε)-approximation bound is very loose; no analysis explaining why empirical K-means solutions achieve near-optimal performance; importance weighting in Theorem 1 lacks theoretical justification

Gradient-based variants require careful tuning despite claims of stable configuration; Authors manually identify hyperparameters across datasets; using plain instead of weighted MSE (Section B.2) appears ad-hoc rather than principled

Non-negligible data requirements for gradient variants (Table 7: 5k vs 1k samples); while augmentation helps, this practical limitation is underexplored and reduces applicability in data-scarce FL settings

Experimental setup concerns: sharded splits with disjoint classes are somewhat artificial; fusion dataset selection varies across experiments; Transformer OTFusion dramatic failures (near-random) lack clear explanation of root cause
Limited scope: no large language model experiments despite claiming generality; missing analysis of when fusion is preferable to alternatives; privacy-utility tradeoffs in FL not examined

Presentation could be clearer: many algorithm variants without guidance on when to use each; connection between theoretical motivation and fixed-previous-levels assumption underexplained; level partitioning heuristic lacks sensitivity analysis
